Although I did get tricked by “Curry complements” because I did not notice the spelling, and was thinking “Just the right amount of spice!” Or maybe “He was a great actor, we will miss him” (since Dolly got a call-out, why not Tim?)

And double bonus points for the Reds call out, though they haven’t been doing so well this year. There was an old joke we used to say about Cleveland but alas it fits for us this year: Why doesn’t Columbus have a Major League Baseball team? Answer: because then Cincinnati would want one too.

SRO = Standing room only!!! As a Brit, I had no idea. Never came across this in real life. Only in the NYT crossword, where i have got (sorry, gotten) used to plugging it in alongside Oreos (which i have never tasted) and IHOP (which i long thought was something to do with the Easter bunny). I was trying to guess what SRO meant… i thought it might be some play on “sorry”, but i guess that’s unlikely in corporate America. 

I finally assumed it meant “sold right out”. Now i know!

Are you actually allowed to stand in theatres (sorry, theaters) in America? (Not sure if we’re talking “movie” theaters —aka cinemas?) I would think health and safety regulations would mean everyone must have a seat?

RE SRO: I first started doing crosswords in the 1980s. My mother was a big crossword puzzle devotee, so everytime I do one today I remember her. 

Anyway, back then it became apparent to me that some answers that were -- well -- "puzzling" to me were easy for her.  I came to believe that ofttimes puzzle answers (and their clues) were geared towards those who were at least a generation older than I. At that time, I had an extensive background in films of the 1930s and 40s, so some answers came more quickly to me than to my contemporaries.  I would compare crosswords with my mother and ask "How do you know that?". Her reply: "Everybody knows that!" (A conversational strategy I would employ when playing trivial pursuit - and that's a clue to how old I am! 

So SRO is not a common phrase now. But in my mind's eye, I can still see movie scenes of newspapers coming off the press describing a hit film as "SRO" - Standing Room Only. It has become a phrase these days only kept alive by crossword puzzles, but at one time was a part of the common vernacular.

Do I love word quirks?  OH ,BUT I DO.  And seeing a new word formed by taking the same letter twice out of another word – four times! – thoroughly filled my word quirk quotient.  

Do I Iove wordplay?  OH, BUT I DO.  And DO A DOUBLE TAKE brought a sweet and satisfied smile.

Do I love nifty construction?  OH, BUT I DO.  And fitting four of these pairs in the same box – having them cross! – not to mention having the last letter of one of the long theme pairs abut the first letter of another – twice! – and still fit in a 13-letter revealer and make everything fit symmetry?  Very, very impressive to pull this off.

So, I mightily “Huh!”-ed, and “Wow!”-ed, along with the pleasure of filling in the squares, and left the puzzle thinking, “Ain’t crosswords grand!?!”  Thank you for making this, Ben!

A completely original idea that I would imagine has never been done before.  And very well-executed -- which could not have been easy.  Considering all the constraints of theme positioning and density, it's remarkable that there's no compromised fill in the grid.  All of this is the good news.

The bad news is that the theme was not at all clear to me as I was solving, nor was it needed, -- and therefore I solved it as a themeless.  Why do I have the strongest suspicion that most of you did likewise?  I patted myself on the back for seeing what DO A DOUBLE TAKE meant in the context of the themers and exactly what had been done to the long answer in order to get the short answer.  But none of this occurred to me while solving and therefore my appreciation all came post-solve.  

How does a constructor bring the solver into the process earlier?  He has to make it almost impossible to solve without first figuring the trick out.  

How might that be accomplished in this particular case?  Darned if I know:)   But it's a clever conceit, nonetheless.

Fun bio factoid* for the day:

The AVIAN lineage is not merely descended from dinosaurs -- birds *are* dinosaurs. 

I suspect some of you are already aware of this.

For an excellent and readable treatment of this, check out the recent book by Steve Brusatte: The Story of Birds: A New History from Their Dinosaur Origins to the Present.

It is surprisingly readable, considering it is written by an actual scientist heavily involved in this kind of research. He has also written a couple of other books about dinosaurs that are worth reading. And for those across the pond: Although Steve is a Septic by birth, he is now at the University of Edinburgh.

*Yes, I know. But I want to use the newer, less favored meaning of "factoid." So, don't bother. Your pedantry is not welcome here.

In the 1980's I went to a lot of performances of the San Francisco Opera with SRO tickets.  It was the best way I could afford to go to more operas.  The tickets were cheap, you bought one, staked out a spot in front of the doors, marked it with a coat and asked someone to save your place in line, dashed to McDonald's for a quick sandwich, ate it while you waited, and when the doors opened, everyone rushed inside to find a place at the rails at the back of the house (balcony or mezzanine preferred). As the house lights dimmed and the curtain rose, we scoped out empty seats, and if the seats were still empty at the end of the first intermission, we could take one for the rest of the opera.

Once, when we had a rather insignificant earthquake, the house lights came on, the out-of-towners rushed to the exits, and we had terrific seats for the rest of the opera. 

When the shaking had begun, the soprano was just then singing, "Please don't leave me!" and of course we didn't.

a/ (a clearing, night.)
(2 men, Curry and Sot, in wellies)

Sot: There. Well… that’s that. Date night has been brought into being and The Big Surprise?…. Snow!…. from the air conditioner.

Curry: Air conditioner snow.

Sot: … and no dinosaurs. Yes. Big surprise… No dinosaurs! No-no-no! And no sign of a comeback. Been there, done that.

Curry: d/ You can’t know! 

Sot: a/ True… true. But I do.

Curry: You lie.

Sot: I lie? Oh?..  (reproved) Oh but I tried. I tried.

The (real) Times puzzles are British or cryptic-style. I used to scoot over to the university library to xerox them. But they are very different animals  from US  crosswords.

SAMPLE CLUE: Most inexpensive hat priced in error. (4, 5)
Answer in 10 minutes.

@SBK in TO



ANSWER: DIRTCHEAP
EXPLANATION:
CLUE Part I: 'Most inexpensive' = straight definition
CLUE Part II: 'Hat priced in error' = tricky or wordplay element; anagram HATPRICED to get "DIRTCHEAP"
'In error' is a hint for anagramming. Other hints include: drunk, tipsy, askew, ragged, tossed, thrown, etc.
